newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end sharply higher after tame data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end sharply higher after tame data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities prices ended sharply higher on Thursday following more news that inflation remained well under control.

The July consumer price index showed a modest 0.2 percent increase and industrial production was up 0.2 percent, but capacity utilization fell to 83.1 percent. In addition, real earnings were reported by the Labor Department to have fallen 1.0 percent.
The data helped to reassure investors that little inflationary pressure was likely to be seen soon.
Robert Dederick, chief economist and executive vice president at Northern Trust, said this week's economic data show the rate of inflation remaining at a temperate pace.
"We got some nice numbers from the point of view of the Federal Reserve. Inflation is still well contained," Dederick said.
"We don't even have evidence of problems (with inflation) down the road," he added.
Furthermore, should any signals of inflation crop up, Dederick expected that the Fed would move quickly to contain growth.

"The primary strength in the economy is inventory building. It's good for now, but not necessarily for the end of the year," said David Levy, vice chairman and director of forecasting at the Jerome Levy Economics Institute at Bard College.
"The big question mark now is the consumer. Consumer borrowing has gotten to the point where tighter credit standards are being imposed," Levy said.
Offsetting that somewhat was the "wealth effect" from the strong stock market that has put a lot of cash into the pockets of many Americans, he said.
He said the stock market's runup was unprecedented, thus making the effect of any sustained decline in the market hard to forecast.
"There's a real recognition at the Fed that (economic measurement) is different now than from the 1970s and 1980s," Levy said.

He argued that inflation-adjusted short-term interest rates were currently at the high end of where they traded historically. That factor would give federal policy makers pause before making any further move to tighten monetary policy, he said.
Analysts said the United Parcel Service (UPS) strike was becoming a significant threat to the economy.
They pointed out that if the strike lasts beyond Friday, the nearly 200,000 striking UPS workers currently out of work would not be counted by the August payrolls survey.
The result would be a payrolls increase under 100,000. Such distortions usually can be discounted, but interesting to note.
The Treasury's 30-year issue was ending up 27/32 at 97-19/32 to yield 6.56 percent.

At the short end of the maturity spectrum, three-month bills were up 2/32 to yield 5.19 percent. Six-month bills were unchanged at 5.20 percent and year bills were off four basis points at 5.24 percent.
The 10-year issue was up 18/32 at 98-31/32 to yield 6.27 percent. The five-year was 8/32 higher at 99-17/32 to yield 6.11 percent and the two-year 3/32 higher at 99-31 to yield 5.89 percent.
